sources.claim: A sole proprietorship is not a separate legal entity, so the owner can be held responsible for business debts; an LLC or corporation generally separates owners from business liability; the structure affects taxes and liability, and the SBA suggests talking with an attorney or accountant.

sections.skill: Describe sole proprietorships and general partnerships

questions.prompt: Jo starts selling crafts alone and registers no entity. What is her business most likely?

choices.text: An LLC, created automatically when she makes a sale
A sole proprietorship
A partnership, because she has customers
A corporation, because she sells products to the public

questions.correct_answer: A sole proprietorship
questions.intro: A SOLE PROPRIETORSHIP is one person doing business without forming a separate entity. It is the default: if you sell on your own and do not register another form, you are usually a sole proprietor. It is simple, but the business is not separate from you, so you are personally responsible for its debts. A GENERAL PARTNERSHIP is two or more people doing business together for profit without forming another entity. Partners usually share profits and can each be personally responsible for business debts. Source: SBA guidance; state law varies.
questions.feedback: Doing business alone without forming an entity is usually a sole proprietorship.

sections.skill: You and the business are the same

questions.prompt: In a sole proprietorship, whose debt is the business's debt?

choices.text: The bank's
Only the customers'
The owner's
No one's

questions.correct_answer: The owner's
questions.intro: In a sole proprietorship, there is no wall between you and the business. Picture one wallet: business money and debts are legally yours. If the business owes a supplier, you owe the supplier. A general partnership is like several people sharing that same wallet: each can be on the hook for what the business owes. Forming an LLC or corporation is how some owners try to build a wall, but that is a separate step with its own limits.
questions.feedback: Owner and business are the same legally.
